findings.description: AWS access key ID and secret access key are hard-coded in plaintext in the instance user_data script, exposing long-lived credentials to anyone with access to instance metadata, console, or Terraform state, and risking leakage via logs or version control.
Ingress rule allows TCP port 22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing administrative access to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.

Ingress rule allows TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0. Combined with public subnet placement and automatic public IP assignment, this fully exposes the web server to the internet with no compensating controls (e.g., WAF, TLS termination).
map_public_ip_on_launch = true automatically assigns public IP addresses to instances launched in this subnet, increasing the attack surface by exposing resources directly to the internet by default.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true automatically assigns public IP addresses to any instance launched in this subnet, expanding the attack surface unnecessarily.

The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true, so data stored on this volume is not encrypted at rest, risking exposure of sensitive data if the underlying storage or a snapshot derived from it is compromised or shared.

The snapshot is created from the unencrypted portal_server_disk volume and inherits its unencrypted state, so backed-up data remains unencrypted at rest and could be exposed if the snapshot is shared or made public.

The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (no aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration), leaving potentially sensitive network traffic metadata unencrypted at rest.

findings.issue_category: missing access controls / public access block
findings.description: No public access block, bucket policy, or ACL restricting access is defined for this bucket, and force_destroy is enabled, risking accidental exposure or deletion of flow log data without explicit access restriction.
